title: The court case duration model: the whole pipeline in one notebook
intro_html:
IDSE (CS3006) project. This notebook takes real Indian court records from the raw download all the way to the model you can try at otlr.vercel.app/model. At every step it says what we did, why, and what we found.

Our question. Court cases in India often take years. We wanted to know which cases take long, where, and whether we can tell on the day a case is filed. The answer is meant for planning, for example to estimate how many of this year's new cases will still be pending next year. It is not a prediction for any one person's case.

The short answer. We can tell which type of case will be quick. But for real disputes, what we know on the first day says very little about which ones will finish fast, and most of a dispute's time is spent after its first hearing.

The notebook has two parts:

  • Part A, the data: the question, where the data came from, what was wrong with it, how we cleaned it, two problems that would have fooled us, how we made the yes/no answers, and what the data shows.
  • Part B, the model: what the model is allowed to see, how we split the years, the simple rules it must beat, the three models we tried, the one we chose, how well it does on cases it never saw, what it relies on, a few extra analyses, its limits, and two real cases run through it.

Every number here is calculated from the cleaned data (data/clean/10/) or read from the result files our scripts wrote (reports/*.json). No number is typed in by hand. Slow steps (the random forests, the shuffle test) are not run again; their results are read from the reports. All code is the project's own package in src/courtcases/.

Data: Development Data Lab's judicial data (eCourts, cases filed 2010–2018), licence ODbL v1.0.

stages.title: The question
stages.intro_html:
Why this question. Courts need to plan: how many judges and staff they need, and which cases legal-aid offices should try to settle. For that they need to know which kinds of case take long, and where.

What we ask. One clear question the model can answer:

If we only know what is written on the day a case is filed in a Tamil Nadu district court, how likely is it to finish within one year?

"Finish" means the case ended in that court: a judgment, a dismissal, a settlement, a Lok Adalat, or the file closed because the accused ran away. If the case was sent to another court, it has not finished; it is still going on somewhere else.

Why yes/no and not "how many days". Many cases had not finished when the data was collected, so we do not know their total number of days. But we can answer "did it finish within a year?" for every case we could watch for at least a year (step A7 shows how).

stages.title: The data and where it came from
stages.intro_html:
What. Development Data Lab (DDL), a research group, collected the records from the government's eCourts website, removed people's names, and published one row per case for every district court in India, for cases filed from 2010 to 2018. The data comes as one big folder: one file of cases per year (16 GB in total), one file with the law and section of each case, and small "key" files that turn number codes (such as the case type) into words.

How we got it. The folder can only be downloaded all at once, as one very large stream. Our script scripts/fetch_ddl.py reads the stream as it arrives, keeps only the files we need, checks that each file arrived without errors, and stops early. Then scripts/build_dataset.py turns the files into a smaller, faster format (Parquet). It reads every column as text, because a code like "01" would become 1 as a number and then no longer match the key files.

Licence. The licence file in the download is ODbL v1.0, which lets us use the data as long as we credit it.

stages.title: The raw mess, before cleaning
stages.intro_html:
What. Before fixing anything, we measured what was wrong. Five problems, each shown below with real values from the data:

  1. Missing values are hidden as blanks and as special codes: -9998 means "unclear" and -9999 means "missing".
  2. Impossible dates: decisions in the year 0001 or 7201, the fake date 5000-01-01, and cases "decided" before they were filed.
  3. One law, thousands of spellings. Court staff type the law names by hand: 29,857 different spellings for a few dozen laws.
  4. Court names are typed by hand too, with spelling mistakes ("trail", "musif", "subardinate").
  5. Section numbers are free text: "138r/w142", "OVIIR1".

Why measure first. A wrong fix is worse than an honest "unknown", so every cleaning rule in the next step reports how many rows it changed.

stages.title: Cleaning, with before and after counts
stages.intro_html:
What. Each problem gets one small function in src/courtcases/, and every function has tests (142 tests in total, run with uv run pytest):

  • Law names: make them lower-case, keep only the letters, then match them against a list of patterns, from the most specific to the most general. A name that matches nothing stays "Other"; we do not guess.
  • Section numbers: keep the main section: "304(B)" → 304B, "138r/w142" → 138, "OVIIR1" → Order 7.
  • Court names: matched to 15 court types; "Other / unclear" if nothing matches.
  • Dates: any date outside 1950–2022 is removed and counted; cases "decided before filing" are marked.
  • Special codes: -9998 → "unclear", -9999 → "missing".
  • How a case ended (52 codes): each code is put in one group: decided, settled, dismissed, disposed, dormant, moved (sent to another court: it left, it did not end), interim (bail orders) or missing.

Why these choices. We never "fix" a wrong date (we cannot know what it should have been) and we never guess a law; we count what we could not fix. A moved case is not counted as finished, because counting transfers as endings would make courts look faster than they are.

The code below runs the real functions and prints how much each one changed.

stages.title: When was the data collected?
stages.intro_html:
What. The data does not say when it was collected, but we need that date: if a case has no decision, we only know it was still pending on that day. There is a clue. The number of decisions recorded each month is steady for years, then suddenly drops. That drop is when the data was collected.

How. Our function cutoff.cliff looks for the first lasting drop: the first month where that month and the next two are all below half of a normal month (a normal month is the middle value of the twelve months before it). We use "half" because the collection happened during February 2019, and a half-collected month would make decided cases look pending. We do this for each district, and use the state's date when a small district's numbers are too uneven to tell.

A mistake we fixed. Our first version used "the last normal-looking month" and put Tamil Nadu's date in July 2020, which was wrong: after the collection a few courts kept adding records, and that small trickle started to look "normal". We changed the rule and added a test so the mistake cannot come back.

stages.title: The early years are incomplete
stages.intro_html:
What. Take only the Tamil Nadu courts that already existed in 2010 and count their cases by filing year. The same courts have 3.6 times more cases filed in 2018 than in 2010, and the share of cases decided on the same day they were filed grows from under 1% to 18%.

Why this matters. Courts did not get 3.6 times busier. When a court started using computers, its pending cases were entered, but most cases that had already finished quickly were not. So the early years are missing their quick cases and look much slower than they really were. (This is called survivorship bias: only the long cases "survived" into the records.) So the model only uses cases filed from 2015 to 2017.

stages.title: Labelling "finished within a year" without guessing
stages.intro_html:
What. For every case, our function target.label records two things: how many days we could watch it (until it ended, until it was sent to another court, or until the data was collected), and whether it finished in this court during that time. If a case was still pending when the data was collected, we only know it lasted at least that long.

Then each case gets an answer to "finished within 365 days?": 1 (yes), 0 (still pending after 365 days) or unknown. We only give an answer to cases filed at least one year before the data was collected, so that every labelled case had a full year to finish. A case sent to another court before day 365 stays unknown.

Why this rule. Our first version labelled every case it could. For cases filed in 2018, the quick ones had already finished and were labelled "yes", while the slow ones were still pending and could not be labelled at all. So 2018 came out more than 90% "within a year", which is clearly wrong. The code below shows that mistake and then the correct labels.

display(lab["unusable"].value_counts().drop("", errors="ignore").rename("cases").to_frame())

stages.title: Where the time goes in a real dispute
stages.intro_html:
What. Steps A1–A8 show how long cases take. This step looks at where the time goes, for real disputes: every case except petty-offence cases and bail-type petitions, which usually end in days. We split each case at its first hearing:

  • Waiting for the first hearing: from filing to the first hearing.
  • After the first hearing: from the first hearing to the end, using Kaplan–Meier so that cases still going are counted, not dropped.

We also look at the gap between a case's last hearing and its next hearing date, and at the stage each case had reached at its last hearing, for cases still pending when the data was collected.

Why the model can't use this. Hearing dates happen after filing. Using them to predict on the filing day would be cheating, so we use them here only to describe what happens.

Data quality. Checked first (cases filed 2015–2017): 4.7% of first-hearing dates are blank and 0.3% are before the filing date (both left out here). In 80% of finished cases, the last hearing date is the same as the decision date. The data has only one gap between hearings for each case, so the number of hearings below is a rough estimate.

stages.title: The inputs: only what is known on filing day
stages.intro_html:
What. Each case is turned into 12 inputs (features.build and features.add_law), in two groups:

Basic filing facts

  • the district, the type of court, the type of case (the court's own code, for example os = civil suit, cc = a criminal case before a magistrate) and the month of filing;
  • how busy the courts are, using only earlier cases: how many cases were already pending in that district's courts of that type on the filing day, how many they finished in the year before, and how many cases of the same type were filed there the year before. (We use the logarithm of these counts, so going from 10 to 100 counts as much as going from 100 to 1,000.)

The law and section (what the case was filed under)

  • the law, the law and section together (the 40 most common, for example "Negotiable Instruments Act section 138" = a bounced cheque), whether the offence is bailable, whether the case is criminal or civil, and how many sections of the Indian Penal Code were charged.

What we left out on purpose. Hearing dates and what each hearing was for (they come from the case's future), the decision date and how the case ended (that is the answer itself), the gender of the people in the case (a public tool should not judge a case by gender), and the court number (a visitor can't know which numbered court will get the case).

Why this matters. If a model sees information from the future, its test scores look great but it fails in real use. This mistake is called leakage. For the same reason, the list of case types and sections the model knows is decided using the training years only.

stages.title: The time split: learn from the past, test on a later year
stages.intro_html:
What. The models learn from cases filed in 2015; we use cases filed in 2016 to pick the best one; the winner then learns again from 2015 and 2016 together and is tested once on cases filed in 2017, which it has never seen. Cases from 2010–2014 are left out (step A6).

Why not mix the years randomly. The model will be used on future cases. If we mixed the years, the model would learn things about 2017 (such as how fast courts had become that year) and look better than it really is. Testing on a later year is the fair test, and it also shows whether things change over time (step B12).

stages.title: Simple rules to beat, and how we score a prediction
stages.intro_html:
What. Three simple rules (baselines) that any model must beat. Each learns from 2015–2016 and is tested on 2017:

  1. Overall rate: give every case the same chance.
  2. Rate by case type: look up the share for that type of case.
  3. Rate by case type and district: a look-up table by type of case and district. (Small groups are pulled towards the overall rate, so a group of three cases can't give a silly answer.)

How we score predictions. For each case the model gives a chance (a probability) of finishing within a year.

  • Accuracy: say "yes" when the chance is 50% or more, and count how often that is right.
  • AUC: pick one case that finished within a year and one that didn't. AUC is how often the model gives the first one the higher chance. 0.5 is guessing, 1.0 is perfect.
  • Brier score: how far the chances are from what really happened (the average of (chance − result)², where the result is 1 or 0). Lower is better; always saying 50% gives 0.25.
  • Log loss: also lower is better, but it punishes confident mistakes much more (for example, saying 95% for a case that dragged on). We used log loss to choose the model.

stages.title: Three kinds of model, with and without the law inputs

What. We tried three kinds of model, each with a few settings, on both groups of inputs (scripts/train_within_1y.py):

stages.title: The model we chose, and why
stages.intro_html:
What. We set the rule before looking at 2017: use whichever model had the lowest log loss on 2016 after learning from 2015. That was logistic regression with the law inputs (with the setting C = 1.0, which controls how strongly the weights are kept small).

stages.title: Extra analysis: predicting the number of days (linear regression)
stages.intro_html:
What. The main model answers yes/no because unfinished cases have no known number of days. A regression (which predicts a number) needs finished cases, so scripts/regress_days.py answers a smaller question, and says so: for cases that finished within 730 days (two years), how many days did they take? It learns from 2015 cases and is tested on 2016 cases. It predicts log(1 + days), because a few very long cases would otherwise dominate. The rule to beat is the typical (median) number of days for that type of case.

Why this is only a side analysis. It only describes cases that did finish within two years. It says nothing about the many that did not, so it must not be read as "how long your case will take".

stages.title: How long cases stay pending (Kaplan–Meier curves)
stages.intro_html:
What. For Tamil Nadu cases filed 2015–2018, the share of cases still pending after a given number of months, using the Kaplan–Meier method (survival.kaplan_meier). Each day it looks at the cases still being watched and how many of them ended that day, and keeps a running product: S(t) = Π (1 − dᵢ/nᵢ), where dᵢ cases ended on day i out of nᵢ still being watched. A pending case is watched until the data was collected and then simply stops being counted; a case sent to another court stops at its transfer. We never guess what happened after we stopped seeing a case.

What the method assumes. It assumes that the reason we stopped watching a case has nothing to do with how soon it would have ended. That is true for the collection date; for transfers it is only roughly true.

stages.title: Limitations
stages.intro_html:
What. scripts/experiments.py tested the chosen model in four ways; the results are read here.

  1. Inside one type of case it is weak. Within a single case type the AUC is only 0.49–0.62 for rent, domestic violence, maintenance, execution, marriage and civil-suit cases. The model knows which types of case are quick, but between two cases of the same type it can barely tell.
  2. Things change over time. Courts got faster every year, so a model that learned from 2015–16 expects slightly too few quick cases in 2017. Giving 2016 more weight barely helps.
  3. Other time limits. The same method for "within 6 months" and "within 2 years" also beats the case-type rule, so the result is not special to one year.
  4. Collection-date rule. A stricter and a looser version of the collection-date rule give the same 2017 results.

summary_html:
Part A, the data. 81 million raw court records, read as text. We cleaned 29,857 spellings of law names, hand-typed court names and sections, impossible dates and special codes, using small tested rules that count every change. Two facts shaped everything: the data was collected in January–February 2019 (found from the sudden drop in monthly decisions, for each district), and the early years are missing their quick cases, so we only model cases filed 2015–2017. "Finished within a year" is only given to cases that had a full year, which fixed a mistake that made 2018 look more than 90% "quick".

Part B, the model. Twelve facts known on the filing day, nothing from the future, no gender. Learn from 2015, choose on 2016, test once on 2017. Three kinds of model against three simple rules: the law inputs matter far more than which model we use. Our logistic regression is right about 8 times in 10 on 549,273 new cases (AUC 0.873, Brier 0.138, against 0.844 and 0.163 for a look-up table), and its chances match reality. But most of that comes from easy cases: on real disputes it is right 74.3% of the time, against 72.0% for always guessing the most common answer (B7), and models trained only on disputes do no better. The filing day tells us the type of case and not much more; most of a dispute's time comes after its first hearing (A9). Inside one type of case the model is weak, and courts got faster each year. The regression on days and the district groups are side analyses, and we report them as weak. How a dispute ends (B14) depends mostly on the type of case; settlement is rare but can be ranked, and cheque-bounce cases settle far more often than Indian Penal Code cases.
